highlights.title: You Probably Aren’t Going to Get the Plague
highlights.summary: The death of a lab worker in Russia has authorities looking at whether plague played a role. Even if it did, though, the odds of it spreading are very low.
body: A mysterious death of a woman in Russia following a lab accident has stoked fears about plague spreading. But the odds of that actually happening remain very low, with the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention saying on X Tuesday afternoon that the circumstances of the case remain unconfirmed and there is “no indication of a broader threat to the United States” at this time.

“We are working across the US government to assess developments as additional information becomes available,” the agency said. “CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely.”

Last week, a young researcher died from severe pneumonia of “unknown” origin after reportedly breaking a test tube at her workplace, the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute in Siberia. The hospital that treated her before her death was placed under quarantine and her coworkers at the lab were isolated, according to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.

highlights.title: Supercomputing researchers document evolution of AI hardware
highlights.summary: An ongoing survey tracks the latest AI accelerator systems to keep hardware relevant for Lincoln Laboratory staff and sponsors.
body: As artificial intelligence transforms industries and national security, understanding the latest hardware capabilities is important for maintainind technological advantage.

AI accelerators — specialized systems designed to speed up capabilities such as neural networks, deep learning, and machine learning — have been a major area of development for nearly a decade. Since 2018, team from the Lincoln Laboratory Supercomputing Center (LLSC) has been conducting the Lincoln AI Computing Survey (LAICS, pronounced "lace"). Six papers later, LAICS continues to summarize current commercial AI accelerators and compare their peak performance and peak power.

"About eight years ago, we saw a sharp rise in the number of research AI accelerators described in research papers and commercial accelerators being announced, and we started to get questions about them from government sponsors of the laboratory's work. That was motivation enough to start the survey," says Albert Reuther, a staff member at the LLSC, which operates and optimizes the high-performance computing systems used by thousands of laboratory research staff.

highlights.title: OpenAI Is Pissing Off a Bunch of Mathematicians—Again
highlights.summary: “There’s a perception of mobster behavior” from leading AI companies, one mathematician tells WIRED as OpenAI prepares to release more than 100 new solutions to unsolved problems.
body: In August, OpenAI convened around 40 mathematicians to discuss what to do if AI outpaces human capabilities in the field. The company hinted that its powerful models had solved hundreds of long-standing math problems, say people who were in attendance, but company representatives assured attendees it would not release the solutions all at once—an assurance OpenAI spokesperson Lindsay McCallum says the company is “not aware of”—and, worried by how the community might react, sought advice on how to publish the findings.

Attendees responded with “a mixture of excitement and dread,” but the meeting was a promising first step, recalls Northwestern University mathematician Bryna Kra. The group, she tells WIRED, asked the firm not to just publish them in a blog or tweet, like they had done with 10 problems earlier that month. Instead, it would be important for OpenAI to publish papers explaining the work so that mathematicians could absorb, digest, and use the results, according to Kra. “Apparently, that input was ignored,” she says.

highlights.title: Ronaldo breaks silence over Portugal walkout in extraordinary statement
highlights.summary: Cristiano Ronaldo has broken his silence over his Portugal walkout in a lengthy statement in which he says he is not retiring from the national team.
body: The 41-year-old, whose actions had raised doubts over his international future, accused Portugal's new head coach Jorge Jesus of broken promises in a near 2,000-word statement to his 679 million Instagram followers.

Addressing the uncertainty over his Portugal future, the Al Nassr forward said: "If I am physically well, playing for my club, with goals I hope, after serving the suspension that may be applied to me, I will be available, as I have always been until today, to compete and win for our national team."
Portugal boss Jesus, who previously denied there was a rift between him and his captain, said on Sunday the door was still open for Ronaldo to return to the national team.

However, the future of Portugal's record goalscorer and appearance-maker, whose 146 goals in 234 international caps is the most of any men's player in history, is far from clear following his decision to air his grievances in public.

highlights.title: ‘We live in grief-phobic societies’: experts on how to get more comfortable with death
highlights.summary: We are all going to die, and so is everyone we know. So how can you not be terrified? For most people, death is not a standard conversation topic. Once, at lunch, a friend began talking about her mother’s death several years earlier.
body: Afterwards, I asked him what was wrong. “I really don’t like talking about death,” he said, his hands twitching anxiously. “I don’t even like thinking about it. It freaks me out.”
His discomfort struck me as silly – and also the most normal thing in the world. We are all going to die, and so is everyone we know. So why be terrified? And how can you not be terrified?

My friend is far from alone in his discomfort. “We live in grief-illiterate and grief-phobic societies,” says Dr Lucy Hone, a resilience and grief researcher and author of the book How Will I Get Ever Through This?: A Practical Guide to Navigating Life’s Toughest Times.

Hone began researching grief over a decade ago, after the sudden death of her daughter, Abi. On our video call, she wears one of Abi’s old hats, an orange and white beanie with polka dots and a big orange pouf on top. It’s ridiculous, Hone says, but it makes her laugh.

highlights.title: Chris Bourg named vice provost and Barbara K. Ostrom (1978) Director of the MIT Libraries
highlights.summary: Chris Bourg, who has served as director of the MIT Libraries since 2015, has been named vice provost and Barbara K. Ostrom (1978) Director of the Libraries, MIT Provost Anantha Chandrakasan announced today.
body: “The title ‘vice provost’ signals the enduring importance of the MIT Libraries in the digital age,” said Chandrakasan. “While the ways in which the libraries meet the needs of our community might change as technology changes, their mission of protecting access to knowledge and information is as vital as ever.”

Thanks to a generous gift from Barbara K. Ostrom ’78, SM ’78, the position of the director of the libraries now has an endowment to help fund it in perpetuity. Bourg noted that the gift is especially meaningful for her, due to the sense of service she shares with Ostrom: they both completed Reserve Officers' Training Corps (ROTC) during their time as undergraduates — Bourg at Duke University and Ostrom at MIT — before going on to active military service.

highlights.title: The 12 Best Video Game Series of the 1980s and '90s, Ranked
highlights.summary: When we look back on the 20th century and the many great experiences it gave us, we tend to think of a few favorite video games that meant the most to us. But the medium introduced more than just our personal favorites.
body: A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

Can your refrigerator or toaster play Doom? The answer might surprise you. For decades, any devices with a modicum of computing power and a screen of some sort (and even a few things that lack such features) have been used to play Doom, the classic first-person shooter from id Software. The original game gave us a reason to hold LAN parties, introduced us to the depths of hell, and spawned a beloved franchise that in turn has inspired many imitators. Today, the series has fallen out of favor, even factoring in the success of the 2016 reboot and its sequels. But we’ll never forget the juggernaut it once was.

highlights.title: Drones sink ships near NATO countries in “unacceptable” attacks, EU says
highlights.summary: Drones sank two cargo ships and damaged a third in the exclusive economic zones of NATO member countries for the first time, killing at least two sailors. The attacks represent a notable escalation as Black Sea commercial shipping has increasingly come under attack during the Russian invasion of…
body: The Togo-flagged cargo ship Alfa Watan sank, and the Palau-flagged cargo ship Able was set ablaze after being attacked by multiple sea and aerial drones about 80 miles (128 kilometers) off the coast of Bulgaria on October 6, according to the Associated Press. In an interview, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev described the incidents as “an unacceptable attack in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone” and “a blatant violation of international law and maritime law.”

The fate of the Alfa Watan’ s crew was not immediately known after the vessel sank. A Bulgarian ferry managed to evacuate the 18 crew members of the Able, with two severely injured mariners being flown to a hospital in the city of Varna.

This comes one day after drones struck the Turkish-owned cargo ship named Royad Mammadov within Romania’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea on October 5. That ship caught fire and eventually sank, with 11 crew members rescued by Romanian ships and helicopters while one crew member remains missing, according to Euronews. Two crew members were killed.

highlights.title: We can’t just change the definition of ‘recording’
highlights.summary: With AI hardware, tech companies are pushing the definition of what does and doesn't constitute a recording. For most of gadget history, it'd be reasonable to assume that a device with a microphone or camera is either recording you or it isn't; it's either on or off, without much gray area.
body: Tech companies with new AI hardware want you to agree that always-listening, often-recapping devices don’t count as recording.

Last week, Bloomberg ’s Mark Gurman reported that Apple is working on a smart home camera that doesn’t save video recordings. Instead, AI uses the visual data to create text snippets that describe what’s happening around your home. Supposedly, it’ll support facial recognition, but without video footage. The idea is that it still protects some privacy. This tech, Gurman says, is similar to how the cameras in rumored future AirPods will also work.

It’s similar to Apple’s Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4. The Apple Watch has had a microphone for ages, mostly for Siri and taking phone calls from the wrist. Of the four Audio Intelligence features, two have caused the most debate online: Live Rewind and Siri Recap. The former produces a transcript of the past 15 seconds, whereas the latter can generate high-level summaries of the conversations you have throughout the day.
points: With AI hardware, tech companies are pushing the definition of what does and doesn't constitute a recording.
For most of gadget history, it'd be reasonable to assume that a device with a microphone or camera is either recording you or it isn't; it's either on or off, without much gray area.

highlights.title: 'This Needs to Change' — PlayStation Fan Gets PSN Account Hacked and Restored, Acknowledges Others May Not Be as Lucky
highlights.summary: PlayStation fans are questioning the security of their PSN accounts as yet another prominent community member had their account hacked and stolen. Over the weekend, a prominent member of the PlayStation community, known as RealRadec, claimed that his PSN account had been hacked.
body: The situation mirrored one that happened to noted PlayStation podcaster and ex-IGNer Colin Moriarty earlier this summer. Moriarty had his PSN account stolen from him during a livestream, prompting some panic. However, given Moriarty's status in the PlayStation community, he was able to raise a lot of noise and receive assistance from various connections at Sony. Moriarty confirmed during a stream on Monday that he lent that same assistance to Radec, as the two have collaborated on Moriarty's podcasting network, Last Stand Media.
This all led to Radec getting his account back, but he was quick to note that he may not have been as lucky if he didn't have a platform and connections.

"It would be foolish of me not to acknowledge that this was dealt with as quickly as possible because of the position I'm in," said Radec. "Not many people have that reach, and I am fully aware of that. This is a problem that has been brewing for a long time now at PlayStation. No one deserves to have their account stolen from them and lose access to all of their games, DLC, save data, trophies, etc. It's not right. This needs to change."

highlights.title: On the Podcast: Haider Ackermann’s Tom Ford Is About Risk and Freedom
highlights.summary: A few days after presenting his spring 2027 collection for Tom Ford, Haider Ackermann sat down with Nicole Phelps in his Paris office to discuss his latest show, his inspirations, and how he became a fashion designer on “The Run-Through.”
body: They began by talking about desire and seduction. “We’re living in a period where men are more vain than they have ever been before,” Ackermann told Nicole. “And they’re embracing their feminine side. They’re more daring.” He encouraged his models to seduce the crowd and to feel joy as they stalked the runway. He also insisted that the point of all that sexiness wasn’t merely to provoke. “I am interested in taking risks and feeling free, certainly in a world where everything is more puritan and reserved,” he said.

When Nicole noted the dedicated group of friends and customers who go to all of Ackermann’s shows—Tilda Swinton among them—he replied: “I do believe in loyalty. I’m very loyal to all my exes. I don’t know how to dis-love once I have loved.”

Ackermann will soon be off to Chile to go kayaking amid the glaciers. He travels all around the globe, but has a particular affinity for remote places where his cellphone has no service. “It is perhaps in search of silence. When you go very far away and lose yourself and feel so small against Mother Nature, you’re suddenly much closer to yourself,” he reflected.

highlights.title: OpenAI will watermark ChatGPT outputs by default—but only in the EU
highlights.summary: OpenAI will begin automatically watermarking text generated with ChatGPT in the European Union, the company has announced. It will also offer the watermarking feature in other regions, but it will be off by default outside of the EU.
body: The move in Europe is driven by a need to comply with the EU AI Act, which took effect in August. It requires marking content produced by AI models in a way that another tool can detect. Unfortunately, there is still no completely effective and reliable way to do that. A few standards already exist, like SynthID and the C2PA project, but they are relatively easy to circumvent for anyone with basic know-how.

The same is likely true for OpenAI's watermark. Its method is proprietary; the company calls it textGrain, and has published a technical paper explaining how it works. But in general, it works like other LLM watermarking tools we've seen in the past: It puts patterns in the word choices that are not clear to a human reader, and that don't meaningfully change the general quality of the output, but that someone with a key can use a specialized detector to find. OpenAI says it will be giving access to the detector to a limited number of researchers and organizations, and providing a request-for-approval process for others to be added over time.

highlights.title: 12 Biggest GTA 6 Questions the Previews Haven't Answered Yet
highlights.summary: Since Netflix's extended look at Grand Theft Auto 6 debuted back in August, we've heard fairly little from Rockstar Games about 2026's most anticipated video game. That all changed on Sept. 29, when Game Informer shared its 14-page deep dive into GTA 6.
body: While there is surely more information to come in weeks heading up to the Nov. 19 launch, there are plenty of big questions about GTA 6 that we still have no concrete answers for. Here are a few that stand out.

Cheat codes are a foundational element of the Grand Theft Auto series, as much as flashy cars and the Wanted level. However, in all the preview interviews and footage we've seen so far, Rockstar has yet to officially confirm that cheat codes will return in GTA 6.

There's good reason to suspect that they will return, though. Both GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2 included dozens of cheat codes, allowing you immediate access to stylish outfits, infinite ammo, and top-tier vehicles (or horses). Enabling cheats in both games turned off achievements, but Red Dead 2 was a bit more strict in how it implemented cheats, essentially preventing them from being used to progress the main story campaign. Many of the best cheats needed to be unlocked by progressing Arthur's story and purchasing newspapers, and you could save your game while a cheat was active.
